rv.q: Radcliffe doesn’t just do away with the fourth wall, he manages to expand his magical aren’t-people-wonderful optimism to include the whole orchestra, mezzanine and balcony.
Instead, he twinkles through them, and his joy in the work is contagious.
Every Brilliant Thing shatters the format, making it a true breath of fresh air.
Radcliffe is a spark plug, and his interactions with the audience are peppered with charming improvisation.
Thanks in no small part to the radiant emotional authenticity Mr. Radcliffe brings to the role, the narrative maintains our interest
Clearly, everyone here understood all that what was really needed was Radcliffe and what he means to people.
It’s Radcliffe’s vitalizing and vulnerable performance, a cardio workout both physically and emotionally, that’s the reason to go.
The show works because Radcliffe more or less wills it to.
Radcliffe has the audience in the palm of his hand.
Any one-person show is obviously dependent on the magnetism of its performer, and Radcliffe is in total command of both the material and the room.
Radcliffe is so affable a presence and so charming an interlocutor in each of his audience exchanges that the conceit works as well as it possibly can.
I left delighted by the experience, albeit wishing the story had more substance.
Mr. Radcliffe is a huge asset, of course: While I’ve never seen “Thing” in any of its previous incarnations, I can’t imagine a more charming, accessible player for these purposes.
Will they think it still worth it for the chance to see Daniel Radcliffe in this role? I feel they might.
Even an actor of Radcliffe’s enormous charisma and charm can’t help but be buried in the deluge of audience participation that’s about to be unleashed.
How can we not root for Radcliffe as he delivers a tour de force, serotonin-boosting performance that’s as powerful as any drug currently on the market?
The wondrous specificity of the brilliant things, the structure of the script, the palpable energy of the room, and the importance of the message make Every Brilliant Thing a visionary revolution.

The familiar music, touching premise, and Radcliffe’s winning personality combine to create an hour of theatre that, in spite of its subject of depression and suicide, manages in its life-affirming optimism to be both humorous and moving, while steering clear of undue schmaltziness.
It truly feels like we’re all at a party, celebrating life and all the little every day things that make it worth living.
For 70 minutes Radcliffe is arguably delivering the greatest male stage performance of the current New York theater season.
In fact, he’s the living definition of brilliant.
His performance allows for humour without deflection and vulnerability without sentimentality.
Daniel Radcliffe is everything you want in Every Brilliant Thing. Theatre just isn't the venue for it.

cn.t: Critics praise Radcliffe's warmth and interactive energy in this affecting solo show about depression and life's small joys, though some find the audience participation gimmicky. Most laud its emotional resonance despite occasional tonal unevenness.

sg.ra: SeatPlan, TickPick and Headout all converge: center rows D-K sit at a perfect distance to take in the whole stage without craning. Row A is called out as too close for comfortable viewing. Dress Circle overhangs at Orchestra row L and the Mezz overhang only becomes obvious at row R without significantly cutting the stage, so the middle band is protected. 2017 ATG restoration upgraded legroom throughout.

SeatPlan flags Dress Circle A-B center as offering unobstructed sightlines and the 'front few rows of the Center Dress Circle' as premium; rows D-F center are repeatedly called out as great-value seats with full sweep of the stage. The 258-seat section has a good rake and generous legroom. Balcony overhang only becomes obvious at row J and doesn't cut into the stage, so every row is usable.

SeatPlan describes Balcony rows A-B center as hanging close enough for detailed views and reports sightlines 'better than average' for a third level. Rear rows G-H are the cheapest in the house. Rake is very good, but legroom is tighter than the rest of the theater and the top of the stage may be cut by the balcony's angle. AVFMS user at G110 noted that some in-audience action isn't visible from rear balcony.

vr.q: Spending just over an hour in a room with a group of strangers being reminded what it is that you love about theater and also what it is that you love about life.
Every brilliant thing remains a perfect show... I cannot recommend it enough.
Daniel Radcliffe fits the Bill perfectly, giving a performance that significantly elevates what I would not consider a perfect play.
